title: ACA s. 28 — Rules applicable to substance of dispute

content.overview: Section 28 prescribes the substantive law to be applied when the place of arbitration is in India. It differentiates arbitrations other than international commercial arbitration from international commercial arbitration, permits party designation of applicable rules of law in the latter, and requires the tribunal to take the contract and applicable trade usages into account.
content.glance: Section 28 prescribes the substantive law to be applied when the place of arbitration is in India. It differentiates arbitrations other than international commercial arbitration from international commercial arbitration, permits party designation of applicable rules of law in the latter, and requires the tribunal to take the contract and applicable trade usages into account.
content.study:
Module 1: Domestic arbitration
In an arbitration other than an international commercial arbitration, the tribunal decides the dispute in accordance with the substantive law for the time being in force in India.

Module 2: International commercial arbitration
For an international commercial arbitration where the place is in India, the tribunal applies the rules of law designated by the parties; absent designation, it applies the rules of law it considers appropriate in the circumstances.

Module 3: Express authorisation for ex aequo et bono
The tribunal may decide ex aequo et bono or as amiable compositeur only where the parties have expressly authorised it.

Module 4: Contract and trade usages
In all cases, the tribunal must take into account the terms of the contract and trade usages applicable to the transaction.

provisions.title: Rules applicable to substance of dispute

examples.title: Rule applies
examples.body: An international commercial arbitration seated in India contains an express governing-law clause; the tribunal begins with the parties' designated substantive law subject to section 28.

examples.title: Rule fails or changes
examples.body: A tribunal in a non-international commercial arbitration disregards the substantive law in force in India and substitutes a foreign substantive law without a statutory basis.

hypotheticals.question: May a tribunal decide ex aequo et bono merely because it considers that approach fair?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Section 28(2) requires express authorisation by the parties.

distinctions.title: Domestic and international commercial arbitration
distinctions.right: Domestic/non-ICA: substantive law in force in India
distinctions.rows: ICA: party-designated rules of law, or appropriate rules of law absent designation.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming section 28 is only a conflict-of-laws provision.
misconceptions.correction: It also directly governs substantive decision-making and expressly addresses party authorisation, contract terms and trade usages.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What is the core rule in section 28?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Section 28 allocates the substantive-law framework according to the type of arbitration and requires the tribunal to observe the contract and applicable trade usages.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Classify the arbitration first, then identify the applicable statutory rule.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should section 28 be applied in submissions?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Start with the statutory text, identify every condition and then apply the facts to the precise statutory consequence.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Keep the submission statute-led and distinguish discretion, conditions and consequence.
